Introduction The influx of digital technologies, ranging between big data analytics and cloud platforms, artificial intelligence, and Industry 4.0 applications, is essentially changing the way contemporary supply chains work. Organizations in all sectors are undertaking digital transformation (DT) programs to enhance connectivity, sharing of information, and automation of the processes in the supply chain networks, and with this come the prospects of high efficiency and responsiveness (He et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024). Nevertheless, achieving competitive advantages by using digital innovations is not always a matter of time; firms usually have difficulties in transforming new technologies into long-term supply chain competitive advantage (SCCA). This research will address the uncertainty of DT's role in SCCA and the conditions under which these benefits will be realized. More specifically, one should unpack the mediating processes through which the DT capabilities relate to the high-quality supply chain performance results. According to the research conducted by previous scholars, the deployment of improved digital tools is not enough; companies have to ensure the complementary organizational functions to maximize the use of digital investments (Warner & Wager, 2019; Mikalef et al., 2019). This understanding heightens the conceptual and empirical importance of the study of dynamic capabilities (DC), the firm’s capabilities to combine, restructure and refresh resources in the fast-changing environment (Teece et al., 1997; Zabel & O’Brien, 2024) as an intermediary between DT and SCCA. * Corresponding author E-mail address azghoul@aau.edu.jo (A. Theoretically, the investigation of the relations between DT and SCCA as the dynamic capabilities considers the recent scholarly demands to combine the Resource-Based View (RBV) and Dynamic Capabilities Theory (DCT) in the context of competition in the digital era (Teece, 2018). Although the positive aspect of digital transformation in supply chains is becoming increasingly acknowledged, a significant gap in the literature is still present: the contribution of DC as a contributing factor has not been studied sufficiently, especially in the manufacturing industry of the emerging economies (Almajali et al., 2025; Nayal et al., 2022). Multiple studies that have been conducted in the past have been concentrated on direct effects of digitalization on the performance of firms or general competency of a supply chain, including integration and agility, yet have not directly focused on the mediating role of sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring capabilities (Aslam et al., 2018). This gap is the focus of the current research, which aims to understand how dynamic capabilities and supply chain competitive advantage relate in the case of digital transformation among the Jordanian manufacturing companies. By doing so, it provides a more holistic view of the capability development in digitally facilitated supply chains and gives organization-specific contextual insights applicable to organizations in developing economies seeking to execute ambitious digital modernization programs. 2. Literature Review & Hypotheses Development The research has its foundation on the RBV and its development, the DCT. The RBV assumes that the firms gain sustained competitive advantage through the control of valuable, rare, inimitable and non-substitutable resources (Barney, 1991). Historically, these resources included tangible and intangible resources including proprietary technology, human resources with skills and efficient supply chains. However, in the modern digital era, digital technologies themselves are strategic assets that can bring a competitive edge in the event of their successful utilization (Alrawahna et al., 2025; Ivanov and Dolgui, 2021; Li et al., 2018). One example of this is a company that implements a superior analytics system that improves its demand forecasting and inventory management system, and surpasses its rivals that do not implement these systems (Amosu et al., 2024). The lack of dynamism in RBV has however been criticized for its failure to describe how firms constantly develop, renew and recombine resources with environmental turbulence and technological disruption (Helfat et al., 2023). The DCT is the solution to this limitation by focusing on the capability of a firm to integrate, create, and restructure its internal and external capabilities to address the challenges of the rapidly changing environments (Teece, 2007). According to DCT, three main groups of dynamic capabilities are involved, including sensing, seizing, and transforming, that make organizations able to see the opportunities offered by the market, engage resources in an effective way, and restructure operations to remain competitive in the long term (Ellström et al., 2021). Whereas in unchanging settings, performance might be supported by normal resources, in dynamic and digitized settings, dynamic capabilities are required as a means to attain sustained benefit (Al-Moaid & Almarhdi, 2024; Alzghoul et al., 2024). In this theoretical framework, RBV treats digital transformation initiatives, including the implementation of ERP systems, IoT-based production monitoring, or AI-driven analytics, as an important resource in an organization which promotes the operational efficiency and performance of the supply chain (Yu et al., 2025). Nevertheless, DCT argues that only well- developed dynamic capabilities, including process reconfigurations, employee reskilling, and organizational learning, make such digital resources bring actual competitive advantage (Ellström et al., 2021). In this regard, DC can be seen as the activation processes that can transform digital potential into real value (Rizana et al., 2025). On the other hand, DT itself can be strengthening DC by adding to the sensing capacity of firms through real-time market data, seizing capacity through fast- based data-driven decision-making, and transforming capacity by improving interaction and sharing of knowledge across supply chain networks (Dubey et al., 2018; Verhoff et al., 2021). This symbiotic relationship highlights the co-evolutionary character of digital resources and dynamic capabilities, implying that firms that have stronger capabilities do not only exploit the advantage of digital technologies, they also increase their benefits (Yeow et al., 2018; Teece, 2018). DT is a complex construct. In its essentials, it is the application of the most innovative digital tools to provide meaningful changes in the performance or reach of the firms (Vial, 2019). DT in the context of the supply chain involves the implementation of such technologies as the Big Data Analytics, Artificial Intelligence, Internet of Things (IoT), blockchain, robotics, and cloud computing to transform supply chain operations (Widiawati et al., 2025). All of these technologies make up what has been called the digital supply chain - an end-to-end data-integration experience, real time visibility, automated routine operations, and data-driven decisions (Ning & Yao, 2023). Notable dimensions of supply chain digital transformation are: (1) Digital integration - connecting systems and partners on common platforms to facilitate information flow seamlessly; (2) Process automation - applying technologies RFID, IoT sensors and AI to automate tracking, inventory and quality control; (3) Analytics and intelligence - using advanced analytics and machine learning on supply chain data to improve forecasting, risk management and optimization; and (4) Digital business models - rethinking value delivery through e-commerce, platforms-based procurement or direct digital fulfillment channels (Khaddam et al., 2023; Karttunen et al., 2023; Verhoeff et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2024). The applicability of DT to SCCA is discussed in the current case examples and empirical research. Organizations that successfully digitize their supply chain operations can attain significantly enhanced responsiveness, e.g., shorter order S. M. A. Lehyeh and A. Alzghoul /Journal of Project Management 11 (2026) 65 processing times due to real-time monitoring and responsiveness in manufacturing; and efficiency, e.g., reduced costs due to optimization of routes and reduced inventory due to data analytics (Tiwari et al., 2024). As an example, the digital supply chain technologies have been demonstrated to introduce flexibility and agility, allowing companies to react better to the market changes or disruptions (Alfaqiyah et al., 2025; Ivanov and Dolgui, 2021). Online collaboration systems and B2B platforms enhance relations with suppliers and customers and thereby enhance reliability and innovation in the supply chain (Corsaro & Murtarelli, 2024). Nonetheless, studies also caution of difficulties: the mere introduction of new technology may fail or even backfire unless companies change their procedures and educate individuals on that (Cui et al., 2023). This highlights the importance of dynamic capabilities; it is the potential of the firm to actually embrace and implement digital technologies successfully. All in all, DT does not constitute an IT initiative, but an organizational one, which in combination with strategy and capabilities may be a powerful source of supply chain competitive advantage (Verhoff et al., 2021). A competitive advantage within a context of a supply chain is the extent to which a firm's supply chain operations surpass those of its rivals with regards to the most crucial performance metrics resulting in benefits in the marketplace (Aslam et al., 2025). SCCA is usually evaluated in the context of cost leadership (price/cost advantage), quality, reliability of delivery and speed, flexibility, and innovation in the supply chain (Khawka et al., 2024). An example of this would be that one company would gain a cost advantage by having an extraordinarily effective logistics system and procurement, whereas another company would gain a responsiveness advantage by having an extraordinarily agile production system that can bring products faster than competitors or customize those (Susitha et al., 2024). The ultimate outcome of SCCA is seen in customer satisfaction, loyalty and market share growth, which are attributed to the excellent performance of the supply chain of the firm (Khawka et al., 2024). Notably, the competitive advantage in supply chain is not a mere operational excellence but rather, it should be challenging to be emulated by the competitors in order to be maintained (Barney, 1991). This is usually owed to uncommon supply chain practices, technologies and capabilities. Some of the most important factors that lead to SCCA are: cost efficiency (ability to manage the procurement cost, production, and distribution more cheaply than the competitors), time- to-market or responsiveness (willingness to serve customers’ needs and adapt to the market changes quickly), and flexibility (the capacity to deal with a variety of products or volume change efficiently), as well as reliability (the ability to meet the promises of quality and delivery in a consistent manner) (Khawka et al., 2024; Susitha et al., 2024). An example is that, a supply chain that routinely produces products at a faster and reliable rate than the market can set high prices or get more shares, which represents a competitive advantage in terms of responsiveness and reliability. Researchers in recent years have looked at the role of well-developed supply chain strategies and technologies with regards to SCCA. To illustrate this point, the close collaboration with suppliers and customers has been closely linked with enhanced flexibility and performance in terms of delivery (Giraud-Carrier et al., 2025). It has been demonstrated that the implementation of supply chain analytics and digital tools can enhance the quality and efficiency of decisions and, therefore, add to the cost and responsiveness benefits (Dubey et al., 2018). Nonetheless, one of the recurrent themes is that technology alone is insufficient, and the improvements require other supporting organizational processes and capabilities to turn them into sustainable competitive advantage (Corsaro & Murtarelli, 2024). This can be contrasted with the RBV concept that around the use of the resources it is the distinct capabilities that make inimitability. One of the elements (e.g., adoption of a similar ERP system) may be replicated by a competitor, but without the ability to provide the integrated processes or agility (dynamic capabilities) that the focal firm has nurtured, the competitor will not perform as well as before (Al Azzani et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2023). Theoretically, DC allows companies to constantly align their activities with the market environment and to innovate in their supply chain operations, which must result in better performance in comparison with less flexible rivals (Teece, 2007; Barney, 1991). A supply chain that has a strong sensing ability will also be able to foresee the changes (change in customer demand, or new disruptions) and respond before competitors, to be ahead of them in terms of time. With a high agility, a firm is able to respond to opportunities (such as a sudden market boom) or threats (such as disruption of supply) more successfully, thus upholding service levels and cost control than its competitors (Aslam et al., 2018). Essentially, dynamic capabilities enable a supply chain to be efficient and resilient, which are some of the major sources of competitive advantage. This correlation is empirically sustained, Aslam et al. (2020) established that market sensing, supply chain agility and adaptability (as part of dynamic supply chain capabilities) all enhanced the supply chain ambidexterity and performance of the firm. Moreover, earlier studies on RBV reveal that the companies that have higher learning and adaptive abilities have long-term advantages in performance since they can innovate and speed up faster than rivals (Kero & Bogale, 2023). DT is an organizational process of radically enhancing business processes, business models, and performance with the help of digital technologies (Verhoef et al., 2021). In contrast to mere IT adoption or digitization, DT is a comprehensive change that extends to strategy, operations, and culture by using different technologies, including IoT, AI, and cloud computing to generate new value (Alhanatleh et al., 2024). DT in the supply chain area takes the form of initiatives such as end-to-end supply chain visibility systems, demand forecasting advanced analytics, and digital platforms between suppliers and customers (Song et al., 2025). These changes can facilitate the sharing of more information, integration of processes, and agility through the supply chain. SCCA can be described as a capacity of a firm to provide better performance in the key performance areas of the supply chain - such as less cost, better quality, more flexible, and quicker reaction to market variations (Zhou & Getele, 2025). The supply chain that delivers high value (in form of reliability, speed, and cost-efficiency) gives it a sustained competitive advantage that the competitors would find difficult to imitate. The successful use of digital innovations in the current environment is becoming 66 the key to achieving SCCA, and the examples of companies that utilize real-time data and automation to significantly reduce lead times and enhance customization can demonstrate this (XiaoWen & Atour, 2025). DC are those abilities of the firm to intentionally form, expand, or alter the resource base, in other words, higher-order capacities to enable the organizations to sense opportunities and threats, to exploit opportunities by mobilizing resources, and to reconfigure assets in response to changing environments (Teece, 2007). The DC in the supply chain are converted into such abilities as supply chain sensing (gathering intelligence about the market), agility (adapting procurement, production, and logistics quickly to the situation), and adaptability (re-aligning partnerships and processes with changing conditions) (Aslam et al., 2018). Such abilities assist a company in its constant innovation and adaptation to the external dynamics hence being able to preserve its competitive edge in the long run (Zhang et al., 2023). The recent literature on digitalization focuses on digital dynamic capabilities, which refer to particular abilities required to incorporate and re-format digital technologies and data into the business processes (Dubey et al., 2023). Integrated digital supply chains can be used to respond to customer orders far quicker by sharing the demand data promptly over the network and initiating production and delivery almost instantly (Wu et al., 2024). Moreover, quality and reliability can be enhanced with the help of DT because of higher monitoring (e.g., sensor-based quality control) and predictive maintenance, therefore, providing a competitive advantage in terms of uninterrupted delivery and product quality (Ivanov & Dolgui, 2021). Empirical evidence is provided by a number of studies such as Nayal et al. (2022) has revealed that digital transformation had a remarkable positive impact on many supply chain capabilities that, in turn, influenced the competitive performance of a firm in the environment of a circular economy. According to Ning and Yao (2023), the digital transformation enhances sustainable competitive advantage through better responsiveness and coordination of the supply chain. Furthermore, in the case of manufacturers that apply Industry 4.0 solutions, their productivity and customer responsiveness have significantly increased, which has become a source of both cost and differentiation advantage (Huang et al., 2023). DC in the supply chain management setting takes different shapes. The first type is the capability of supply chain sensing, which is the possibility to have early indicators of demand shifts, supply shocks, or new technologies through scanning the environment and receiving timely information (Dubey et al., 2018). Companies possessing a good sensing ability can anticipate changes (e.g. in customer preference or maybe a supplier problem) and be prepared in advance. Supply chain agility is also another variant that can be described as the capacity to respond quickly to the changes by adapting the supply chain tactics and operations (Alshaar & Alkshali, 2024). Agility is a DC whereby there is flexibility in the manufacture or quick rerouting of logistics or redirecting resources to handle unexpected demand surges or declines. Another closely related dimension is the adaptability or configurability - the ability to reorganize the supply chain, changing the supplier base, redesigning the supply network, or the introduction of new distribution channels - in the response to long-term changes (Alzate et al., 2024). These dynamic capabilities combined have been referred to as the supply chain ambidexterity, the capacity to be efficient and flexible, to deal with stability and change at the same time (Aslam et al., 2018). DT collides with DC in the digital age in interesting ways. On the one hand, digital tools can be used to facilitate the development of dynamic capabilities, e.g., data analytics is a tool to enhance the sensing capability by giving predictive information (Dubey et al., 2023; Leso et al., 2024). Conversely, new digital technologies need to be implemented and integrated with the help of dynamic capabilities (Warner & Wager, 2019). The process of re-engineering and re-learning may also be necessary in organizations to achieve the promised benefits of digital systems. To give an example, when the supply chain is traced with the help of a blockchain, competitive advantage can only come when the firm is able to reorganize its contracts and information-sharing routine to take advantage of the blockchain capabilities (Wan et al., 2020). Thus, it can be seen that DC both impacts and is impacted by DT. The relationship between the DT and SCCA is mediated by DC. This is the premise based on the combination of the RBV/DCT theory and the patterns of the empirical data mentioned above. Although DT influences SCCA, the research did not ignore the possibility that such an effect can actually be indirect. As a company is being digitally transformed, it is bringing new technologies and processes. These transformations can enhance the performance only as long as the company develops or develops the capabilities (sensing, agility, etc.) to capitalize on them (Teece, 2018). Therefore, the researchers anticipate that an enormous percentage of performance improvement of DT will be achieved through DC. Other researchers give similar results: Mikalef et al. (2019) discovered that the impact of big data analytics (a side of the digital transformation) on the performance was entirely mediated by dynamic and operational capabilities, so the technology did not enhance the performance unless it was applied to the processes of the creation of the capabilities. Similarly, Chatterjee et al. (2023) demonstrated that the quality of decisions was enhanced by big data management that produced a decision-making capability based on big data (a dynamic capability of the company). Dubey et al. (2023) established in the literature on the sustainable supply chain that the influence of analytics on the sustainable supply chain performance was mediated by the dynamic capability (in that case a learning capability). The results of these studies are close to our argument: dynamic capabilities are the developmental outcomes of the digital transformation that is dynamic in nature and leads to the achievement of competitive advantage. According to the literature, DT is a more and more essential strategy forwarded by the firms in pursuit of supply chain excellence, and dynamic capabilities are required to achieve the maximum value of digitalization (Verhoff et al., 2021; Dubey et al., 2023). Previous research is united in thinking that agility, adaptability, and sensing abilities can greatly enhance supply S. M. A. Lehyeh and A. Alzghoul /Journal of Project Management 11 (2026) 67 chain performance and resilience particularly in turbulent environments (Aslam et al., 2018). It is also agreed that such capabilities can be improved using digital tools that offer improved information and automation (Ivanov and Dolgui, 2021). Nevertheless, their inconsistencies and gaps are still there. Not every company investing in the digital transformation can become a competitor, indicating that internal processes (such as organizational preparedness and capability building) are what make one a winner and another a loser (Ning & Yao, 2023). Although DC is theoretically regarded as such a differentiator, there are very limited empirical studies that explicitly relate all three constructs (DT, DC, and SCCA). Most empirical studies concentrate on the two-way relationships, or consider other mediators like integration, which has created a gap in the knowledge of the full triadic relationship between DT, DC, and competitive advantage (Mikalef et al., 2019). Additionally, a large portion of the evidence has been derived under the context of the developed economy (US, Europe, China) and high- tech sectors. The Middle East/Jordanian environment, where the manufacturing companies are vigorously attempting to digitize as part of the country's modernization, has not been properly represented in the high-quality research. The Economic Modernization Vision (2022-2033) of Jordan explicitly addresses digitalization of industries to propel competitiveness but little is known regarding empirical realization of how the Jordanian firms can convert digital investments into competitive advantage (Almajali et al., 2025). The research fills these gaps, giving a consistent view of the mediating purpose of DC in the DT and SCCA connection, and investigating it within the context of Jordanian manufacturing companies, giving new regional data to the Western-centric literature. Thus, the following hypothesis are proposed: H1: Digital transformation has a positive effect on the firm’s dynamic capabilities. H2: Dynamic capabilities positively influence supply chain competitive advantage. H3: Digital transformation has a positive direct effect on supply chain competitive advantage. H4: Dynamic capabilities mediate the positive relationship between digital transformation and supply chain competitive advantage. 3. Methodology The research design adopted in this study was a quantitative, cross-sectional survey-based research design to test the hypothesized relationships between DT, DC, and SCCA. A structured questionnaire was designed, which allowed the statistical analysis of the hypothesized mediation model. The cross-sectional design was considered appropriate because the research is on the prevailing state of DT, DC, and SCCA in companies and theoretical assumption of the relative contemporariness of the relationships between these constructs. The research is conducted using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) and AMOS to find the quality of the measurements and the structural paths (including mediation) in the model proposed. On the whole, this design is appropriate in testing our theory-driven model since it can be used to test several latent constructs and indirect effects in a single cohesive analysis to produce strong evidence of the relationships (Hair et al., 2019). The research target population was the Jordanian manufacturing companies, that is, in manufacturing industries with a high likelihood of having initiated a DT initiative (i.e. pharmaceuticals, electronics, food and beverage, chemicals and textiles manufacturing in Jordan). The manufacturing sector was chosen as the central piece of the study since it is the heart of the Jordanian economy and is in the process of becoming digital and adopting Industry 4.0 in order to stay more competitive. The research captures organizations with critical supply chain performance and where the efforts of DT (such as automation, ERP systems, supply chain IT) are ongoing to stay regionally competitive by focusing on manufacturing firms. The sample frame consisted of the firms listed on the Amman Stock Exchange in the industrial sector and the members of the associations of the national industries. The research was focused on mid- to large-size manufacturing organizations, which presumes that the latter have better formalized supply chain functions and capabilities to invest in digital projects. Overall, 450 questionnaires of survey were sent by email to the managers of the supply chains, operations directors, IT managers, and other top-level professionals of these companies familiar with digital initiatives and supply chain deliverables. The key informants in each of the firms were identified through a purposive sampling approach. Out of the 450 survey mails that were issued, we got 326 survey responses. The obtained sample (N = 326) can be deemed as strong to conduct the analysis of SEM and be general enough to reflect the manufacturing situation in Jordan regarding the size of the firm and subsectors. It encompasses businesses in different areas of manufacture and it is diverse in terms of products and complexity of the supply chain. The items used in the study were back translated to make sure the Arabic version is accurate. To minimize biases, the study promised participants that there were no correct and incorrect answers but they must respond according to the real practices and perceptions. Multi-item Likert measures were used to measure the three primary constructs of the study (DT, DC, and SCCA) based on the previous validated measures. All the scale items were statements that respondents responded to through a 5-point Likert scale (1 = "Strongly Disagree, 5 = Strongly Agree). Multi-item scales improve reliability and simultaneously address the scope of every construct. 4. Results The research was conducted with AMOS software, which engaged structural equation modeling of the survey data of 326 manufacturing companies in Jordan. The measurement model could be tested by confirmatory factor analysis with the use of AMOS and the structural pathways hypothesized could simultaneously be used. The measurement model was initially evaluated on the basis of sufficient fit and validity after which the structural model was evaluated on the basis of hypothesis 68 testing which involves the mediation analysis. The structural equation model had sufficient fit to the data as indicated by various goodness-of-fit indices that fall within the recommended levels (Sathyanarayana & Mohanasundaram, 2024). Particularly, the chi-square to degrees of freedom (CMIN/DF) ratio was 2.534, which is less than the typically recommended cut-off of 3.0 of acceptable model fit (meaning the chi-square is approximately 2.5 times the degrees of freedom, which indicates a reasonable fit between the hypothesized model and the observed data). The other fit indices also indicated a good fit model, since the Goodness-of-Fit Index (GPI) was 0.925, and the Adjusted Goodness-of-Fit Index (AGFI) was 0.904, which is above the 0.90 indicator of a good fit. The Normed Fit Index (NFI) was 0.911 and Comparative Fit Index (CFI) was 0.933 which is greater than 0.90 and, therefore, the covariance in the data is well explained by our model compared to a null (independence) model. Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI) of 0.914 again above 0.90 also confirms the presence of a good fit. Lastly, the Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA) was 0.061 and it falls within the standard range, 0.06 usually represents a close fit. The RMSEA at 0.061 shows that there is a minor approximation error in one degree of freedom. These indices (CMIN/DF, GFI, NFI, CFI, TLI, RMSEA) have acceptable values and in most instances satisfy the requirements of a good model fit as it is noted in the literature of SEM (Hair et al., 2019; Sathyanarayana & Mohanasundaram, 2024). It is thus concluded that the measurement and structural model is a reasonable illustration of the data and confidently proceed to interpret the reliability, validity, and path coefficients. For instance, the moderately strong correlation between DT and SCCA (0.738) indicates firms with more advanced DT tend to have higher SCCA, but the fact that 0.738 < 0.784 suggests that Digital Transformation is not identical to SCCA, there is still unique variance captured by each. Additionally, the study ran the Heterotrait-Monotrait (HTMT) ratio test as a robustness check for discriminant validity, and all HTMT ratios were below the conservative threshold of 0.85, further indicating discriminant validity. In summary, Table 2 demonstrates that our three constructs are related yet sufficiently distinct, justifying their separate treatment in the model. Fig. 1. Discussion This study set out to investigate whether DC mediates the effect of DT on SCCA in Jordanian manufacturing firms. All four hypotheses (H1 through H4) were confirmed by the data. First, our result that DT positively affects DC (H1) is in line with Warner and Wäger (2019), who, via case studies, described digital transformation as an iterative process of capability-building and strategic renewal. The research offers quantitative data to support their story, in fact, on a wide sample, it was found that digitally more developed companies were more likely to claim that they possessed higher dynamic capabilities. This confirms the idea of digital dynamic capabilities, which suggests that new capabilities are created when companies continue to adopt digital tech. It is also consistent with the results of Ellstrom et al. (2021) who found that the application of a digital strategy required dynamic re-alignment of processes (similar to the construction of DC). In the case of H2 (DC and SCCA), the findings are in line with recent empirical studies that have highlighted agility and adaptability within the supply chains. To illustrate, Dubey et al. (2023) assumed that dynamic capabilities mediate or moderate the impact of tech on performance and they discovered that the resilience and performance were enhanced by capabilities such as analytical agility. This direct relationship between DC and SCCA agrees with Dubey et al. (2018) who discovered supply chain agility and adaptability as more effective performance (in their case, sustainable performance). On the same note, Agility and market sensing was found to improve the supply chain ambidexterity (balance between efficiency and flexibility) that is correlated with competitive advantage (Aslam et al., 2018). Yet, the lower coefficient that we had on H2 (b 0.18) than on H3 (b 0.59) indicates that dynamic capabilities may not be as endogenous as they are on performance in our study. Perhaps this subtlety can be explained by the fact that manufacturing is the business sector where the physical enhancements of the processes through the use of technology are quite effective in terms of cost/time, but the capabilities enhance the former strategies even more. Earlier research such as Wamba et al. (2017) established that dynamic capabilities (such as flexibility) are very instrumental in transforming big data analytics to performance. The partial mediation result resembles that, dynamic capabilities have a vehicle role in tech-to-performance conversion, which was supported by other studies like Mikalef et al. (2019), which determined that dynamic and operational capabilities had a mediating role in IT impacting competitive performance, and Shamim et al. (2019) which determined that big data had effect on decision quality mediated by dynamic capabilities. In comparison to Verhoeff et al. (2021), who offered a multidisciplinary perspective on the results of digital transformation, the study provides empirical data on one of the outcomes that had been implied by their authors: enhanced internal capabilities S. M. A. Lehyeh and A. Alzghoul /Journal of Project Management 11 (2026) 71 and performance. Verhoff et al. (2021) emphasized that digital transformation is a process that demands organizational structure and capabilities to change, the findings indicated that such changes (capabilities) indeed occur and are performance- related. Besides, the information echoes with Teece (2018) who suggested that the digital age necessitates dynamic capabilities to ensure a competitive advantage. The research results offer empirical support: companies that integrate DT and DC are presumably those that maintain their competitive advantage, which is synergy in the relationship between technology and strategic management. The correlation between DT and SCCA (0.738) is high, meaning that in the sample of the study, digital leaders are frequently performance leaders. This can be attributed to the findings of Ning and Yao (2023) who discovered that direct impacts of digital transformation are positive on the supply chain competitive performance, and Zhao et al. (2023) who identified that digitalization of the supply chain positively influences resilience and performance through mediators. The partial mediation shows that dynamic capabilities account for a large but not all of such correlation. Other potentially contributing parallel mediators, such as supply chain integration or analytics-powered decision-making (operational capabilities) may also have a role to play perhaps (Chen et al., 2022) mediate DT to performance with supply chain integration mediation. The unique feature of the study is that it deals with DC, but it agrees with other studies such as Dubey et al. (2020) who have taken into account various mediators (such as integration and DC). Perhaps, integration and DC mediate in its entirety, a hypothesis to be tested in the future. Contrarily or as an extension to previous research, in the emerging market setting, digital transformation is a determining competitive force even in Jordan, assumed to be lagging in technology use. This confirms the results of international research (Diaz-Arancibia et al., 2024) according to which the digital transformation is not a process only of the developed world, the advantages are universal, but the formation of capabilities is determined by circumstances. The article contributes to the literature by demonstrating the way in which the pursuit of Industry 4.0 in a developing economy can be reflected at the firm level in the form of better abilities and competitive edge. However, it is worth noting that our findings support the ideas of Almajali et al. (2025): the adoption of digital and internal preparedness results in performance returns, which is compatible with the institutional theory and the RBV in emerging markets. The contributions of the study are that dynamic capabilities are explicitly added to such an equation. The findings support the significance of dynamic capabilities in the literature of strategic management by demonstrating that it is a key factor in the provision of benefits of new digital technologies. This adds to the body of knowledge by filling the gap between the digital innovation and the traditional theory of competitive advantage by the mediating variable of capabilities. To the managers and practitioners, the research is a clear warning: to maximize the use of digital transformation in attaining competitive advantage, an organization should develop a culture of agility and learning that is able to detect changes as they happen and adjust its supply chain approaches in response. The companies which implement the latest digital solutions and robust dynamic capabilities are very likely to be industry leaders, and the companies which ignore the aspect of capability may turn out that costly technologies cannot bring sustainable advantage. Within the framework of Jordan and other emerging economies, the results of this research serve as a way of industrial development: the integration of technology with capacity building can assist these economies to jump to a new competitiveness level. The study contributes to the theoretical and practical debates on the transformation of the digital supply chain through the evidence that the dynamic capabilities are not merely a complementary element but a required mediating variable in gaining the competitive advantage in the digital era. Lastly, the results of this research support the paradigm according to which dynamic capabilities are the key to digital transformation success. They confirm that the dynamic capability of the organization is essential in transforming the promise of digital technologies into the supply chain sustainable competitive advantage. It adds to academic literature through synthesizing concepts in the RBV, DCT, and digital business literature and empirically supporting those, and it adds to practice by informing firms on where to center their transformation efforts. Finally, the study notes that in the modern rapidly changing business environment, dynamic capabilities are becoming as significant as (possibly more so than) tangible resources, the driver of competitive performance in a digital change era. 6. Conclusion The aim of the research was to investigate the effects of digital transformation on the supply chain competitive advantage and, in particular, whether dynamic capabilities mediate this relationship. Based on the Resource-Based View and the Dynamic Capabilities Theory, the work hypothesis was that although the digital transformation may have a direct impact on the performance of the supply chain of a firm, much of the effects are mediated through the improvement of the dynamic capabilities of the firm (its capacity to sense opportunities, grasp them and reorganize resources). Digital transformation was revealed to greatly enhance supply chain competitive advantage and significantly, dynamic capabilities mediated this outcome in part. Companies that experienced more digital transformation were also claimed to have better dynamic capabilities which again resulted in better competitive results (cost efficiency, responsiveness, flexibility, etc.). The important observation of this paper is that balancing digital transformation and dynamic capabilities vision has never been considered to explain competitive advantage. It is a new addition to the knowledge that is being added through this integration on the issue of capability-based competitiveness in the realm of digital disruption. The study synthesizes the previous literature on the topic, which already recognized that the digital transformation enhances performance and that dynamic capabilities play an important role in long-term advantage; it establishes the connection between these two threads and shows how they intersect. It emphasizes that the concept of dynamic capabilities is not merely theoretical but practical assets that will increase the 72 returns of digital investments. To scholars, it brings a tested model that provides a nuanced insight to the literature on strategic management and operations through demonstrating that such value of digital resources is achieved through complementary organizational capabilities. As a practitioner, it highlights that to get the full potential of digital transformation, agile and adaptive processes and cultures have to be developed at the same time. The emphasis on the Jordanian companies also focuses on the extrapolation of the management theories to an emerging market environment, as the research employs the concept of empirical data that the principles are applicable outside of the Western paradigm. It also helps strategic efforts in upcoming economies to update the industries with digital technologies, but advises that these updating should also entail human and organizational capacity development. Going forward, future studies may expand these results by examining the effects of these factors longitudinally, other mediating variables (such as knowledge management practices or supply chain integration) and potential moderators (such as environmental uncertainty or organizational structure) that may guide the digital transformation-dynamic capabilities-performance nexus. The other opportunity is to implement this framework in other industries or areas or at a network of supply chain level (how does an inter-firm dynamic capability, such as collaborative agility, moderate the impact of digital supply chain integration on network performance). Moreover, qualitative research may ask further questions of how exactly dynamic capabilities are developed in the context of digital transformation (e.g., what are the key learning routines or decision-making that transform). The present research highlights an important piece of information that needs to be conveyed to the theory and practice in the modern business environment: digital transformation and dynamic capabilities go hand in hand. Companies that embrace new high levels of digital technologies and fail to develop the competencies to effectively utilize them can only make modest gains, but those that embrace the combination of technology with agility, learning and adaptability can reap transformative competitive advantages. The results underscore the fact that dynamic capabilities are the driving force behind the aspect of adaptability which helps a firm to always stay ahead in terms of competitive advantage despite the rapid changes in technology. Businesses that keep in mind to transform dynamically will be the ones that achieve long-term success as they rise to the challenges involved in the industry 4.0 and beyond. References Al Azzani, H. JSON: Name: dt_dc_scca_mfg Title: Structural equation modeling of digital transformation's mediated effect via dynamic capabilities on supply chain competitive advantage in manufacturing firms in an emerging economy Short Hypothesis: Digital transformation increases supply chain competitive advantage in manufacturing firms by enhancing the firms' dynamic capabilities. Related Work: Existing studies examine links among digital transformation (DT), firm performance, and capabilities via three main patterns: (1) direct DT→performance models that report positive correlations but do not explain mechanisms; (2) capability-centric studies showing dynamic capabilities (DC) improve supply‐chain outcomes but often treat DT as a background enabler; and (3) mediation work in analytics/big-data domains that finds DC or operational capabilities mediate technology→performance effects. Limitations across the literature include reliance on bivariate or two-stage analyses rather than an integrated triadic model, predominant focus on developed‐market or single‐case evidence, frequent use of cross‐sectional self‐report measures without robust common‐method controls, and sparse testing of alternative mediators or network‐level effects. Consequently, the specificity and magnitude of DC's mediating role between DT and supply chain competitive advantage (SCCA) remain under‐validated across manufacturing contexts in emerging economies. Abstract: This research tests whether digital transformation (DT) improves supply chain competitive advantage (SCCA) through firms' dynamic capabilities (DC) in manufacturing firms in an emerging economy. We propose a cross‐sectional, theory‐driven mediation model and estimate it using structural equation modeling to quantify direct DT→SCCA effects and indirect DT→DC→SCCA pathways. The main contribution is an integrated, empirically validated decomposition of DT's impact into capability formation and residual direct effects, clarifying how much competitive advantage is attributable to capability enhancement versus direct digital mechanisms. Expected outcomes include (1) statistically significant positive DT→DC and DC→SCCA paths, (2) a measurable indirect effect of DT on SCCA through DC, and (3) estimates of remaining direct DT effects after accounting for DC. Results will provide precise effect sizes for managerial prioritization of capability investments during digital initiatives and strengthen theory by operationalizing DC as the key conversion mechanism for digital investments into supply‐chain competitiveness. Experiments: Datasets: Primary dataset = structured survey of supply‐chain/operations/IT managers from manufacturing firms in an emerging economy (target N ≥ 300; stratified by subsector: pharmaceuticals, electronics, food/beverage, chemicals, textiles). Secondary dataset (optional) = firm-level performance indicators from public filings for construct validation. Measurement: Use validated multi‐item Likert scales for DT (12 items), DC (8 items), and SCCA (7 items); translate/back‐translate instruments. Baselines/Models: (A) measurement model (CFA); (B) direct model DT → SCCA; (C) mediation model DT → DC → SCCA (full mediation); (D) partial mediation model DT → SCCA + DT → DC → SCCA; (E) alternative mediation model replacing DC with supply chain integration or operational capability. Evaluation metrics: model fit indices (CFI, TLI, RMSEA, SRMR), standardized path coefficients (β), p‐values, R^2 for endogenous constructs, effect sizes (f^2), indirect effects with bias‐corrected bootstrap 95% CI (5,000 resamples), mediation proportion (indirect/total). Experimental setup: perform CFA and reliability tests (CR, AVE), assess discriminant validity (Fornell‐Larcker, HTMT), test for common method bias (Harman single factor, marker variable), estimate structural paths in AMOS or equivalent SEM software with maximum likelihood estimation, compute bootstrapped indirect effects. Comparisons/ablations: (1) compare β_DT→SCCA between models B and D to quantify mediation attenuation; (2) replace DC with alternative mediator in model E to test mediator specificity; (3) multi‐group SEM by firm size (small vs. medium/large) and by subsector; (4) sensitivity ablation removing items with loadings < 0.65 to test measurement robustness. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Causality limits: cross‐sectional design prevents definitive causal claims; observed mediation indicates statistical mediation but not temporal causation. 2) Common method and self‐report bias: manager surveys for DT, DC, and SCCA may inflate correlations and produce measurement bias. 3) Representativeness: sample frame limited to one emerging economy's manufacturing firms may limit external validity to other countries or service sectors. 4) Omitted variables: unmeasured confounders (e.g., supply chain integration, organizational culture, regulatory environment) can bias path estimates. 5) Multicollinearity: high correlation between DT and SCCA may reduce precision of mediation estimates and inflate standard errors. 6) Measurement validity: translated scales may have differential item functioning across subgroups. 7) Sample size constraints: complex SEM with multiple latent variables requires adequate N; underpowered models risk Type II errors. 8) Generalization to network level: firm‐level results may not extend to inter‐firm supply‐chain network dynamics. 9) Model mis‐specification: alternative model structures (reciprocal effects, omitted moderators) may better fit the true data‐generating process.
